Black Friday weekend is a major test for American retail, and three chains built for it also pay shareholders every quarter. Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT), Target (NYSE:TGT) and TJX Companies (NYSE:TJX) each raised full-year guidance in their latest reports, each covers its dividend from operating profit, and each has raised its quarterly payout in recent years. Target pays the highest yield of the three at 2.6%. That makes this group a fit for retirees who put dividend safety and regular increases ahead of a big starting check.

courtesy of Wal-Mart Stores Inc.
Walmart: Trillion-Dollar Scale Behind a Rising Payout

Walmart yields 0.71% at a recent price of $131.94, the lowest starting income in this group. The quarterly dividend is $0.2475 per share, up from $0.235 in 2025 and $0.2075 in 2024.

Dividend safety: Coverage is wide. Walmart pays a trailing dividend of $0.965 per share against diluted EPS of $2.76, and its free cash flow yield of 1.42% exceeds its dividend yield. In the fiscal third quarter, the company paid $2.0 billion in dividends and still bought back $2.7 billion of stock, after producing $7.77 billion in operating income. The dividend record shows quarterly payments going back to 1999. The per-share rate rose every year from 2000 through 2023 and rose again in both 2025 and 2026.

Kroger (KR) raised its dividend 11% to $0.39 a quarter, its 20th straight annual increase, and free cash flow covers the payout nearly three times.

Walmart (WMT) and Costco (COST) are growing faster than Kroger, but investors pay up: Walmart trades near 48 times earnings versus Kroger's 13.

Shoppers trading down cut identical sales growth to 0.2%, and Greg Foran says customers are buying "fewer items in the basket."

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

The Federal Reserve's Beige Book, released November 25, found households still "price sensitive and increasingly selective" about discretionary purchases. That puts the focus on Kroger (NYSE:KR), which raised its quarterly dividend 11% to $0.39 per share. According to the company, the increase marks its 20th consecutive year of dividend raises. Retirees have to ask whether that payout can keep growing while shoppers put fewer items in their carts.

jetcityimage / iStock Editorial via Getty Images
A Dividend Record That Holds Up

Kroger's payment history matches the streak claim. The company paid $0.065 per quarter in 2006. The rate then rose every year, reaching $0.32 in 2024, $0.35 in 2025, and $0.39 now. At the recent price of $69.82, the forward dividend of $1.56 a year works out to a yield of about 2.2%.

Kroger has plenty of room to pay it. The $1.56 is 30% of the midpoint of its reaffirmed adjusted EPS guidance of $5.10 to $5.30. Paying it on all shares outstanding costs about $921 million a year. Management expects free cash flow of $2.7 to $2.9 billion, so even the low end covers the dividend about 2.9 times. Debt is also manageable. Net debt to adjusted EBITDA was 1.91, below Kroger's own target range of 2.3 to 2.5.

title: Walmart, Amazon Face Surprising Shopping Shift
detail:
Walmart, Amazon Face Surprising Shopping Shift
Moz Farooque ACCA

WMT
AMZN
CRM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Americans are increasingly using Black Friday discounts to stock up on everyday necessities rather than simply splurging on holiday gifts, signaling a shift in consumer spending that could favor retail giants Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) while putting pressure on retailers heavily dependent on discretionary purchases.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 7 Warning Sign with WMT.

Is WMT fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

WMT GF Value chart

Persistent inflation and household budget concerns are changing how Americans approach the holiday shopping season, with artificial intelligence emerging as an increasingly important tool for bargain hunters.

According to Adobe Digital Insights, U.S. consumers spent $82.5 billion online between Nov. 1 and Nov. 22, representing a 9.1% year-over-year increase.

However, the composition of that spending tells a more revealing story.

Online sales of personal hygiene products jumped 40% compared with October's average, while household cleaning products and basic clothing registered increases of 33% and 27%, respectively.

Meanwhile, Salesforce data showed November discounts were 8% deeper than last year, pushing average merchandise selling prices 1% lower.

AI-assisted shopping is also gaining momentum.

Walmart CEO John Furner recently revealed that customers using its AI shopping assistant, Sparky, spent 40% more per order than other shoppers. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy reported that American customers using Alexa spent 50% more than nonusers.

Investors Takeaway

Adobe expects Black Friday online spending to jump 9.2% to $12.9 billion, followed by $15.1 billion on Cyber Monday.

However, strong headline sales may conceal growing pressure on retailer profitability.

Walmart's exposure to essential merchandise could give it a competitive advantage over discretionary-focused retailers such as Target (NYSE:TGT).

Investors should closely monitor merchandise mix, comparable sales, gross margins and inventory levels in upcoming quarterly reports.

Additionally, Walmart and Amazon's AI shopping investments could become meaningful revenue drivers if higher customer spending translates into incremental sales and sustainable profitability rather than simply reflecting the purchasing habits of existing high-spending customers.

Shares of Walmart Inc. WMT have gained 3.6% since the company reported its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Nov. 19. The retail giant's resilient business performance, sustained market share gains, growing contribution from higher-margin businesses and raised fiscal 2027 outlook appear to have bolstered investor confidence.

Over the past year, Walmart shares have advanced 20.9%, outperforming the industry's gain of 20.1%, the Zacks Retail – Wholesale sector's rise of 3.3% and the S&P 500's growth of 4.7%. However, WMT has lagged prominent retail peers Target Corporation TGT and Dollar General Corporation DG, whose shares have rallied 91.8% and 28%, respectively, while outpacing Costco Wholesale Corporation COST, which has advanced 19.7% during the same period.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Walmart's ability to attract customers across income groups through competitive pricing, a broader merchandise assortment and enhanced shopping convenience has been instrumental in sustaining its growth momentum. With shares gaining ground following its quarterly results, should investors capitalize on the momentum or wait for a more attractive entry point? A closer look at the company's fundamentals, challenges, valuation and earnings estimate revisions may offer some clarity.

What's Driving Walmart Stock Higher?

Walmart's solid third-quarter fiscal 2027 performance underscores the strength of its evolving business model. Total revenues increased 5.2% year over year to $188.8 billion, while adjusted earnings per share rose 4.8% to 65 cents. Adjusted operating income grew 5.5% on a constant-currency basis, outpacing constant-currency net sales growth of 4.4%. Walmart U.S. comparable sales, excluding fuel, increased 2.9%, supported by higher transactions and average ticket size. The company recorded some of its strongest grocery market share gains in three years.

Walmart's thriving e-commerce business remains central to its growth strategy. Global e-commerce sales increased 17%, with Walmart U.S. recording 23% growth, marking its 11th consecutive quarter of growth exceeding 20%. U.S. store-fulfilled deliveries jumped more than 40%, while expedited deliveries grew more than 50%. Its extensive store network, expanding third-party marketplace and AI-powered shopping capabilities are strengthening customer engagement and enhancing operational efficiency.

Beyond traditional retail, Walmart is increasingly benefiting from higher-margin businesses, including advertising, membership and marketplace services. Global advertising grew 25%, while membership fee revenues increased 17%. Improving e-commerce economics and a favorable business mix helped Walmart U.S. achieve e-commerce incremental margins exceeding 12%. The newly introduced $120 annual membership bundle combining Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus offers further opportunities to deepen customer loyalty and capture a greater share of household spending.

Encouraged by its performance, Walmart raised its fiscal 2027 constant-currency net sales and adjusted operating income growth guidance to 4.9-5.2% and 8-8.6%, respectively. Adjusted earnings are now projected between $2.84 and $2.89 per share.

General Motors Is Up 11% in a Month as the Nasdaq-100 Fell 10%. Is Its Nasdaq Switch Really That Good? ©PhonlamaiPhoto's Images and yangwenshuang from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

General Motors stock is up 11% in the past month, mostly on its move to Nasdaq, while the Nasdaq-100 fell 10%.

Ford's higher profit floor and a shift out of Tesla helped too, but Ford expects flat 2027 profit.

At 6.0x forward earnings with a $20 billion buyback, GM still looks like a buy ahead of its 2027 outlook in late January.

General Motors (GM:NASDAQ) stock is up 11% in the past month, while the Nasdaq-100 fell 10%. Most of the gain came from its move to Nasdaq, where it began trading on Nov. 17, in time to make the cutoff that Walmart missed last year for the Nasdaq-100's December reshuffle. If GM gets in, index funds that track the Nasdaq-100 would have to buy the stock.

Ford (F:NYSE) helped too, raising the floor of its profit outlook a day after GM's news. And investors moved money from Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) to Detroit after the Nov. 3 midterms.

Ford's raise came with a warning

On Oct. 28, Ford raised the low end of its 2026 adjusted EBIT guidance to $10.5 billion from $10 billion. But it expects 2027 profit to be about flat, and analysts have its normalized EPS at $1.89 for 2026 and $1.87 for 2027. GM faces the same squeeze: CFO Paul Jacobson put its 2027 commodity headwind at roughly $2 billion.

Tesla lost what Detroit gained. It trades at 180x forward earnings and fell after Nov. 3 on worries that a Democratic Congress could slow a possible merger with SpaceX. Money that moved on politics can move back just as fast.

Still about 6x earnings

Analysts expect GM's normalized net income to stay near $12 billion a year through 2028, so EPS growth comes from buybacks, including a new $20 billion authorization. Consensus has normalized EPS climbing from $10.60 in 2025 to $16.16 in 2028:

General Motors (GM): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (TIKR)

The new listing shouldn't move those estimates. GM still trades at 6.0x forward earnings, near its five-year average of 5.7x:

General Motors (GM): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

The $101 consensus target is about 6.3x GM's 2028 EPS estimate, so the stock only needs those estimates to hold to get there.

TIKR tracks 25 analysts on General Motors. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on General Motors, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See General Motors' Analyst Ratings

Watch January's outlook

So the Nasdaq switch is worth a one-time lift from index funds, and little more. GM still looks like a buy, since every share it retires at 6x earnings lifts EPS. On Nov. 18, GM said it aims to improve on this year's results in 2027 despite inflation. A late-January guide above 2026's $15 billion EBIT-adjusted midpoint would back that up, while one that leans on cheaper steel and copper would leave the stock near 6x.
